title: The Presentation
bigQuestion: How do you build, deliver and defend a five-minute talk in Spanish that an audience will remember?

story.title: Why My Family's Language Matters
story.kicker: A senior in Humboldt Park has to give her capstone talk in Spanish, and the hardest part is not the grammar but standing up and saying what she believes.
paragraphs: Lucía is a senior at a high school near Humboldt Park, on Chicago's northwest side. Her grandparents came from Puerto Rico in the 1960s, her parents grew up speaking both languages, and Lucía answers her grandmother in Spanish and her little brother in English without noticing the switch. For her capstone she has to give a five-minute presentation in Spanish, then answer questions from three classmates and her teacher. She has chosen her topic: why her family's language matters.

Her first draft is a page of paragraphs she plans to read aloud. Her teacher hands it back with one note: "No lo leas. Habla." (Do not read it. Speak.) Lucía protests that she will forget everything. "Then you need a thesis you cannot forget," the teacher says, "and three reasons that hold it up." Lucía writes one sentence on an index card: "Sostengo que el español de mi familia es una herencia que vale la pena proteger." (I hold that my family's Spanish is an inheritance worth protecting.)

The three reasons come from her own life. First, her grandmother's stories exist only in Spanish; translate them and the jokes disappear. Second, Spanish is spoken by hundreds of millions of people across more than twenty countries, so the language is a door, not a fence. Third, in her neighborhood, being able to switch languages is a skill that gets people jobs, from the clinic on Division Street to the bank on North Avenue. For each reason she finds one piece of evidence: a story, a number, an example.

On the day of the talk, Lucía speaks from five index cards. She stumbles once, pauses, and keeps going. When a classmate asks whether English matters more for getting into college, she says, "Entiendo tu punto, pero creo que las dos lenguas abren puertas diferentes" (I understand your point, but I think the two languages open different doors), and then explains why. Her teacher's rubric gives her top marks for organization and for defending her thesis. This chapter is the road she walked to get there.
story.think: Lucía's thesis fit on one index card. Why might a thesis you can say in one breath be easier to defend than a paragraph you have memorized?

sections.title: Choosing a Topic and a Thesis

lessons.title: A Topic You Can Stand Behind
lessons.mainIdea: A good presentation topic about the Spanish-speaking world is narrow enough to cover in five minutes and personal enough that you have something to say.
reading: Lucía's first idea was "la cultura latina" (Latino culture). Her teacher asked her how she would cover that in five minutes, and Lucía admitted she could not. Her second idea was "la comida puertorriqueña" (Puerto Rican food), better but still a book. Her third was the one she kept: why her own family's Spanish matters. It was narrow, it was hers, and she already knew the stories. A *tema* (topic) for a five-minute talk should pass that test: you could explain it to a friend in the hallway, and you would want to.

Topics about the Spanish-speaking world come in three shapes, and each one can be narrowed. A place: not "México" but "por qué mi familia celebra el Día de los Muertos en Chicago" (why my family celebrates Day of the Dead in Chicago). A practice: not "la música" but "cómo la salsa llegó a Nueva York" (how salsa came to New York), if you have a source you trust. A question: "¿Debería ser obligatorio el español en las escuelas de Illinois?" (Should Spanish be required in Illinois schools?). The question shape is the easiest to defend, because it forces a thesis.

Two warnings. First, a topic should not claim more than you can prove. "El español es la lengua más bonita del mundo" (Spanish is the most beautiful language in the world) cannot be supported with evidence; "el español me conecta con mi abuela" can. Second, avoid topics where your only knowledge is a half-remembered fact. If you are not sure when or how something happened, either look it up in a source you can name or choose a topic closer to home.

Heritage speakers sometimes think a personal topic is too easy. It is the opposite. A talk about your own family requires you to turn feelings into claims and memories into evidence, which is the hardest kind of thinking. Lucía's teacher told her that the best capstone talks she had heard in twenty years were about a grandmother's kitchen, a neighborhood corner, or a word that only one family used. Choose something you can stand behind when the questions come.

words.d: the topic, the subject — elegir un tema is to choose a topic; masculine despite the -a ending
the presentation — dar una presentación is to give a presentation
the inheritance, the heritage — la herencia cultural is cultural heritage
broad, wide — un tema amplio (a broad topic) will not fit in five minutes; un tema limitado (a narrow topic) will

look.title: Narrowing in Three Steps
look.text: Watch a topic shrink. Step 1: La música latina. Step 2: La música en mi casa. Step 3: Por qué mi papá pone boleros los domingos por la mañana. Step 1 could fill a library. Step 3 fits in five minutes, and only you can give it. Try it: El deporte → El fútbol en mi barrio → ?
look.prompt: Finish the third step for the soccer example and write a step 3 for two more topics: la comida and las fiestas.

check.q: Which topic is narrow enough for a five-minute talk?
choices: Por qué mi abuela me habla solo en español
Todos los países donde se habla español
check.why: One grandmother and one habit can be covered in five minutes; the other three are far too broad.

check.q: What does "¿Debería ser obligatorio el español en las escuelas de Illinois?" mean?
choices: Is Spanish required in Illinois schools?
Why is Spanish required in Illinois schools?
Should Spanish be required in Illinois schools?
Spanish will be required in Illinois schools.
check.why: Debería is the conditional of deber, so the question asks whether it should be required, not whether it is.

check.q: Why is "El español es la lengua más bonita del mundo" a weak thesis for a presentation?
choices: Because it is not written in Spanish.
Because bonita does not agree with lengua.
Because it cannot be supported with evidence.
check.why: A thesis must be defended with evidence; beauty is an opinion nobody can prove, so questions will have nowhere to land.

lessons.title: Writing the Thesis
lessons.mainIdea: A thesis is one sentence that takes a position, opened with a phrase like En mi opinión or Sostengo que, and everything else in the talk exists to support it.
reading: Lucía's index card holds one sentence: "Sostengo que el español de mi familia es una herencia que vale la pena proteger." That sentence is her *tesis* (thesis): the claim the whole talk defends. It has three parts. An opener that marks it as a position: *sostengo que* (I hold that, I maintain that). A subject: el español de mi familia. A claim about that subject that someone could disagree with: es una herencia que vale la pena proteger. If nobody could disagree, it is a fact, not a thesis.

Spanish gives you several openers, and they differ in strength. *En mi opinión* (in my opinion) is the gentlest. *Creo que* (I believe that) and *pienso que* (I think that) are the everyday choices. *Sostengo que* and *afirmo que* (I assert that) are the formal, confident ones you want in a capstone. All of them take the indicative after que, because the speaker is standing behind the claim: "Sostengo que el español es una herencia." Do not let the formality trick you into the subjunctive; "sostengo que sea" is wrong.

The negative versions flip the mood, and that is worth one careful sentence. "No creo que el inglés sea suficiente" (I do not think English is enough) takes the subjunctive sea, because no creo que expresses doubt. Lucía uses that shape once, in her second reason, and it is the sentence a classmate later challenges. Knowing why sea is there lets her answer calmly.

Test a thesis by asking what evidence would prove it and what a skeptic would say. Lucía's skeptic says, "English gets you into college, not Spanish." Her thesis does not claim Spanish matters more than English; it claims Spanish is worth protecting. The skeptic's point does not touch it. A thesis that is narrow and clear defends itself. Write yours on a card, say it aloud ten times, and it will be there when your notes fail you.

words.d: the thesis — the one-sentence claim a presentation defends; it must be something a person could disagree with
I hold that, I maintain that — a formal thesis opener; indicative follows: Sostengo que el español es una herencia
in my opinion — the gentlest thesis opener; use it once, not in every sentence
to assert, to state firmly — Afirmo que… (I assert that…); afirmar has nothing to do with English affirm in the sense of praise
it is worth it, it is worthwhile — vale la pena proteger (it is worth protecting)

look.title: From Fact to Thesis
look.text: Fact: Mi abuela habla español. Nobody can argue. Thesis: Sostengo que las historias de mi abuela solo tienen sentido en español. Fact: Muchas personas en Chicago hablan español. Thesis: En mi opinión, hablar dos lenguas es la ventaja más grande que tiene mi barrio. Fact: Tengo diecisiete años. Thesis: Creo que a los diecisiete años ya es tarde para empezar a aprender una lengua… ¿o no?
look.prompt: Which thesis is the easiest to attack, and what would a skeptic say? Rewrite it so it is narrower.

check.q: Sostengo que el español ___ (ser) una herencia importante.
check.why: Sostengo que states a position the speaker stands behind, so the indicative es follows; only doubt or denial would call for sea.

check.q: Which sentence is a thesis rather than a fact?
choices: Mi abuela nació en Puerto Rico.
Sostengo que los nietos deben aprender la lengua de sus abuelos.
El español se habla en muchos países.
check.why: A thesis takes a position someone could disagree with; the other three are facts nobody would argue about.

check.q: No creo que el inglés ___ (ser) suficiente para mi futuro.
check.why: No creo que expresses doubt and triggers the present subjunctive sea, unlike creo que, which keeps es.

lessons.title: Three Supports with Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Each of three supporting reasons needs its own piece of evidence, a story, a number or an example, and the number must come from a source you can name.
reading: A thesis alone is a slogan. Lucía's teacher asks for three *argumentos* (supporting reasons), and for each one a piece of *evidencia* (evidence). The pattern is simple to say and hard to do: reason, evidence, one sentence tying the evidence back to the thesis. Lucía's first reason is that her grandmother's stories live only in Spanish. Her evidence is a story: the one about the coquí, the tiny Puerto Rican frog, that her grandmother tells with a rhyme. Then the tie: "Sin el español, la rima se pierde, y con la rima se pierde la abuela" (Without Spanish the rhyme is lost, and with the rhyme, the grandmother).

Her second reason is that Spanish is a door to a large part of the world. Here the evidence is a number, and numbers must be handled honestly. Spanish is an official language in twenty countries and in Puerto Rico, and it has hundreds of millions of native speakers worldwide. Lucía says exactly that; she does not invent a precise figure she cannot cite. In a talk, a rounded number with a named source ("según el Instituto Cervantes," according to the Cervantes Institute) beats an exact one from memory.

Her third reason is that in Humboldt Park, switching languages is a job skill. The evidence is an example: her cousin got hired at a clinic on Division Street partly because he could take a medical history in either language. An example does not prove a general rule, and Lucía says so: "Es solo un caso, pero es un caso que conozco bien" (It is only one case, but it is a case I know well). Admitting the limit of your evidence makes the audience trust the rest.

Three is not a magic number, but it is the right one for five minutes: about one minute per reason, leaving time for the opening and the close. Order them by strength, weakest in the middle, strongest last, so the talk ends on its best point. And check that each reason is different in kind. Lucía's are a story, a number and an example; three stories in a row would feel like one long reason.

words.d: the supporting reason, the argument — tres argumentos con evidencia; not a quarrel (that is una discusión)
the evidence — a story, a number or an example that supports a reason; also la prueba
according to — según el Instituto Cervantes; names the source of a number or a claim
the example — por ejemplo (for example); one example supports but does not prove a rule
the case, the instance — es solo un caso (it is only one case)

look.title: Where Spanish Is Official
rows: Countries with Spanish as an official language
Plus Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory
Countries on that list in the Americas
Countries on that list in Europe
Countries on that list in Africa
look.cite: Standard lists of countries where Spanish is an official language; the one European country is Spain and the one African country is Equatorial Guinea
look.prompt: Lucía uses only the first row in her talk. Which other row would most surprise her audience, and how could she say it in one Spanish sentence with según?

check.q: What is the three-part pattern for each supporting reason?
choices: Reason, evidence, a sentence tying it to the thesis
check.why: Every reason needs its own evidence and a sentence that connects that evidence back to the thesis.

check.q: Why does Lucía say a rounded number with a named source instead of an exact figure from memory?
choices: Because a number you can cite is more trustworthy than one you might have wrong.
Because Spanish does not use large numbers.
Because exact numbers are not allowed in presentations.
Because the audience cannot understand numbers in Spanish.
check.why: Evidence must be honest; a rounded figure with a source is defensible, while a precise number from memory may be wrong.

check.q: "Es solo un caso, pero es un caso que conozco bien" shows the speaker doing what?
choices: Admitting the limit of one example while still using it
check.why: The sentence concedes that one example does not prove a rule and explains why it still counts, which builds trust.

lessons.title: Transitions Between Parts
lessons.mainIdea: Transitions such as en primer lugar, en segundo lugar and por último tell the audience where they are in the talk, so they can follow without a page in front of them.
reading: A reader can look back at a page; a listener cannot. That is why a spoken talk needs *transiciones* (transitions): short phrases that announce where the speaker is going. Lucía's first draft jumped from her grandmother's story to the number of Spanish speakers with no warning, and her practice audience got lost. Her second draft added five phrases, and the same audience could repeat her three reasons back to her afterward.

The workhorse set is ordinal. *En primer lugar* (in the first place, first) opens reason one. *En segundo lugar* (second) opens reason two. *Por último* (finally, lastly) opens the third and signals that the end is near. Spanish speakers also use *primero*, *segundo* and *finalmente* in the same slots, and *para empezar* (to begin with) as a warmer version of en primer lugar. Pick one set and keep it; mixing them is not wrong, but it makes the structure harder to hear.

Between the thesis and the first reason, and between each reason and its evidence, other phrases do the pointing. "Para apoyar esta idea" (to support this idea) introduces evidence. "Por ejemplo" (for example) introduces an example. "Esto demuestra que" (this shows that) returns from the evidence to the thesis. "Pasemos ahora a" (let us move now to) is a clean bridge between reasons, and it uses the nosotros command form, which invites the audience along instead of ordering them.

Write each transition at the top of its index card, in larger letters than the rest. When Lucía lost her place in the real talk, she looked down, saw "POR ÚLTIMO" and knew exactly where she was. Transitions do the same thing for the audience that connectors did for the reader in the last chapter, and the test is the same: cover the phrase, and ask whether it promises the relationship that really follows.

words.d: the transition — a phrase that announces the next part of a talk: en primer lugar, por último
in the first place, first — opens the first supporting reason; followed by en segundo lugar
finally, lastly — opens the last reason and signals the close is near
let us move on to — a nosotros command (from pasar) that bridges two parts and invites the audience along

look.title: Lucía's Five Cards
look.text: Card 1: Tesis: Sostengo que el español de mi familia es una herencia que vale la pena proteger. Card 2: EN PRIMER LUGAR: las historias de mi abuela; el coquí. Card 3: EN SEGUNDO LUGAR: veinte países; según el Instituto Cervantes. Card 4: POR ÚLTIMO: mi primo, la clínica de la calle Division. Card 5: EN CONCLUSIÓN: proteger la herencia; una pregunta para ustedes.
look.prompt: Which card has the least written on it, and why does that not matter? Add one transition to card 2 that would introduce the coquí story as evidence.

check.q: Which phrase would open the third and last supporting reason?
check.why: Por último means finally and marks the last reason; the other phrases open the first reason or introduce an example.

check.q: What does "Pasemos ahora al segundo argumento" mean?
choices: I will pass on the second argument.
You must skip the second argument.
Let us move now to the second reason.
check.why: Pasemos is the nosotros command of pasar, let us move; it bridges to the second reason and includes the audience.

check.q: Which phrase brings the talk back from the evidence to the thesis?
check.why: Esto demuestra que (this shows that) is the tie-back; the others order reasons or introduce an example.

lessons.title: The Conclusion
lessons.mainIdea: A conclusion restates the thesis in new words, gathers the three reasons in one breath, and ends with a line the audience will carry out of the room.
reading: The last thirty seconds of a talk are the ones the audience remembers, and they are the seconds most speakers throw away with "y eso es todo" (and that is all). A *conclusión* has three moves. First, restate the thesis in different words, so the audience hears it fresh: Lucía opened with "una herencia que vale la pena proteger" and closes with "un tesoro que no pienso perder" (a treasure I do not intend to lose). Second, gather the reasons in one sentence. Third, end on a line that lands.

The gathering sentence is where the connectors from the last chapter earn their place. "Por lo tanto, por las historias de mi abuela, por los millones de personas que hablan esta lengua y por las puertas que abre en mi barrio, sostengo que…" (Therefore, for my grandmother's stories, for the millions of people who speak this language, and for the doors it opens in my neighborhood, I hold that…). One sentence, three reasons, one por lo tanto that has been earned by everything before it.

The final line can be a question, a callback or a short quotation. Lucía chose a callback: she returned to the coquí rhyme and said its first line in Spanish, then stopped. Silence for two seconds, then "Gracias." A question works too: "¿Qué historia de su familia se perdería si se perdiera la lengua?" (What story of your family would be lost if the language were lost?) Notice the if-sentence pattern, imperfect subjunctive in the si clause and conditional in the result, carrying real weight in a real talk.

Two things to avoid. Do not introduce a new reason in the conclusion; the audience cannot weigh it, and it makes the three reasons feel unfinished. Do not apologize: "perdón por mi español" (sorry for my Spanish) tells the audience to doubt everything they just heard. Say your last line, say gracias, and stand still until the questions start.

words.d: the conclusion — en conclusión (in conclusion) opens the closing part of a talk
the treasure — un tesoro que no pienso perder (a treasure I do not intend to lose)
would be lost — the conditional of perderse; pairs with si se perdiera (if it were lost)
the question — terminar con una pregunta (to end with a question); hacer una pregunta is to ask one

look.title: Two Endings, One Talk
look.text: Ending A: Bueno, eso es todo lo que tengo. Perdón si mi español no es perfecto. Gracias. Ending B: Por lo tanto, por las historias, por los millones de hablantes y por las puertas que abre, sostengo que el español de mi familia es un tesoro que no pienso perder. ¿Qué historia de su familia se perdería si se perdiera la lengua? Gracias.
look.prompt: Name the three moves in Ending B. What does Ending A make the audience feel about the talk they just heard?

check.q: Which sentence belongs in a conclusion?
choices: Hoy voy a hablar de tres razones.
Por lo tanto, por estas tres razones, sostengo que vale la pena proteger la lengua.
En primer lugar, mi abuela cuenta historias.
Ahora, un nuevo argumento que olvidé mencionar.
check.why: A conclusion gathers the reasons and restates the thesis; introducing a new argument or opening the talk does not belong there.

check.q: ¿Qué historia se ___ (perder) si se perdiera la lengua?
check.why: The si clause holds the imperfect subjunctive perdiera, so the result takes the conditional perdería: would be lost.

check.q: Why should a speaker not say "perdón por mi español" at the end?
choices: Because perdón is an informal word.
Because apologies must come at the start.
Because it tells the audience to doubt everything they just heard.
check.why: An apology undercuts the talk; the audience should leave with the last line, not with the speaker's doubt.

lessons.title: Notes, Not a Script
lessons.mainIdea: Index cards with a few key words per part let you speak to your audience; a full script makes you read to a page.
reading: "No lo leas. Habla." The teacher's note on Lucía's first draft is the whole lesson. When a speaker reads, the eyes drop, the voice flattens, and the audience hears a page instead of a person. When a speaker talks from *apuntes* (notes), the sentences come out a little rougher and a lot more alive. The grammar may be slightly less polished than in the essay; the rubric knows that, and it rewards communication over perfection.

The tool is the index card, la ficha. One card per part: thesis, reason one, reason two, reason three, conclusion. On each card, the transition in capitals at the top, then no more than five key words or short phrases, then any number or quotation you must get exactly right. Lucía's card three reads: "EN SEGUNDO LUGAR — veinte países — según el Instituto Cervantes — una puerta, no una cerca." That last phrase, a door not a fence, is the one line she wanted word for word.

Rehearse from the cards, not from the essay, and rehearse out loud at least three times. The first run will be awful; that is what it is for. By the third run, the sentences that connect the key words will have settled into shapes you can reach for. Time each run. If a five-minute talk comes in at seven, cut a reason's evidence, not the thesis or the conclusion. If it comes in at three, you are rushing; add a pause after each transition.

Heritage speakers often speak Spanish more comfortably than they write it, and the cards let that strength show. Andrés from the last chapter, who needed a six-pass routine to edit his essay, gave his talk with one stumble. Speaking is a different skill from writing, and for many students it is the stronger one. Trust it, keep the cards in your hand, and look at the people you are talking to.

words.d: the notes — hablar con apuntes (to speak from notes), as opposed to reading a script
the index card — one card per part of the talk, with a transition and a few key words
to rehearse, to practice — ensayar en voz alta (to rehearse aloud); el ensayo is both a rehearsal and an essay
to read — an irregular preterite (leyó, leyeron); the teacher's note No lo leas is a negative tú command

look.title: A Five-Minute Time Budget
look.cite: Example plan for a five-minute (300-second) capstone talk, as described in this lesson
look.prompt: Add the rows and confirm they total 300 seconds. Why does the third reason get the most time, and where would you cut first if a rehearsal ran long?

check.q: What does the note "No lo leas. Habla." mean?
choices: Do not read it. He speaks.
Do not leave it. Talk about it.
check.why: No leas is the negative tú command of leer with the pronoun lo, and habla is the affirmative command of hablar.

check.q: What should an index card contain, according to the lesson?
choices: A transition, a few key words, and any number or line needed exactly
Only the thesis, repeated on every card
check.why: Cards hold a transition at the top, no more than five key words, and anything that must be said word for word.

check.q: If a rehearsal of a five-minute talk runs seven minutes, what does the lesson say to cut?
check.why: The thesis and conclusion hold the talk together; trimming evidence from a reason shortens it without breaking it.

lessons.title: Voice, Pace and Pauses
lessons.mainIdea: Speak more slowly than feels natural, pause after each transition, and replace English fillers with Spanish ones or with silence.
reading: In Lucía's first rehearsal she finished in three minutes and forty seconds, and her practice audience caught about half of it. Nerves speed everyone up. The fix is not to speak slowly all the way through, which sounds unnatural, but to plant pauses in fixed places: after the thesis, after every transition, and before the last line. Two seconds of silence feels like ten to the speaker and like nothing to the audience. Mark each pause on the card with a slash.

Fillers are the sounds a speaker makes while thinking. English fillers, um and like, are the first thing a listener notices in a Spanish talk, because they announce that the speaker is translating. Spanish has its own: *este* (roughly um), *pues* (well), *o sea* (I mean), *bueno* (well, okay). A few of these sound natural; a dozen sound unprepared. The better choice is silence. Close your mouth, find the next key word on the card, and go on.

Volume and eyes matter more than most students expect. Speak to the person in the back row, not to the card. Look up at the end of every sentence; that is when the audience decides whether you mean it. Heritage speakers sometimes drop into a fast, quiet register they use at home, which is warm across a kitchen table and lost across a classroom. Lucía's teacher asked her to imagine she was telling the coquí story to her grandmother, who sits in the last row and does not hear well.

Pronunciation is a smaller worry than students think, and the rubric weighs it lightly, but two things help. Say every vowel fully; Spanish vowels do not fade to uh the way unstressed English vowels do. And put the stress where the accent mark tells you: "está," "también," "herencia" on the e, "opinión" on the last syllable. A misplaced stress is the pronunciation error most likely to make a Spanish speaker pause.

words.d: the pause — hacer una pausa (to pause); marked on the card after each transition
the filler word — este, pues, o sea and bueno are Spanish fillers; um and like are English ones
I mean, that is to say — a filler that also introduces a clarification: o sea, la lengua de mi abuela
the pace, the rhythm — hablar con un ritmo tranquilo (to speak at a calm pace)

look.title: The Same Sentence, Three Ways
look.text: Rushed: Sostengoqueelespañoldemifamiliaesunaherenciaquevalelapenaproteger. With fillers: Este… sostengo que, o sea, el español, bueno, de mi familia, es… pues… una herencia. With pauses: Sostengo que el español de mi familia / es una herencia / que vale la pena proteger. // En primer lugar…
look.prompt: Read the third version aloud, holding each slash for one second and the double slash for two. Where would you look up?

check.q: Where does the lesson say to plant pauses?
choices: In the middle of each reason's evidence
After the thesis, after each transition, and before the last line
check.why: Pauses at those fixed points let the audience catch the structure without making the whole talk slow.

check.q: Which of these is a Spanish filler word?
check.why: Pues (well) is a natural Spanish filler; the other three are English and signal that the speaker is translating.

check.q: Which word is stressed on its last syllable?
check.why: The written accent on opinión marks the stress on the final syllable; the other three carry stress on the next-to-last.

lessons.title: Answering Questions
lessons.mainIdea: A good answer repeats the question, replies in two or three sentences, and links back to the thesis; not knowing is allowed if you say so honestly.
reading: The five minutes end and the hard part starts. Three classmates and the teacher will each ask Lucía a question in Spanish, and she has to answer without a card. Her teacher gives her a three-step shape. Step one: repeat or rephrase the question. "Me preguntas si el inglés importa más para la universidad" (You are asking me whether English matters more for college). Repeating buys thinking time, confirms you understood, and lets the rest of the audience hear the question.

Step two: answer in two or three sentences, not ten. A long answer wanders away from the thesis and invites a follow-up you did not plan for. Step three: link back. "Y por eso sostengo que las dos lenguas abren puertas diferentes" (And that is why I hold that the two languages open different doors). The por eso is a small connector doing large work: it tells the audience the answer belongs to the talk.

Some questions will ask for something you do not know. The honest answer is the strong one. "No tengo ese dato, pero puedo buscarlo" (I do not have that figure, but I can look it up). "No estoy segura, pero creo que…" (I am not sure, but I think that…). Notice segura agrees with Lucía; a male speaker says seguro. Guessing a number aloud is worse than admitting a gap, because a classmate may know the real one.

Questions in Spanish use forms you know well: ¿por qué? (why), ¿cómo? (how), ¿qué pasaría si…? (what would happen if…), ¿no crees que…? (do you not think that…). That last one is a trap for the mood: "¿No crees que el inglés sea más importante?" invites the subjunctive in the question, but your answer stands behind a claim, so it takes the indicative: "Creo que las dos son importantes." Rehearse the questions you fear most with a partner, and write your two-sentence answers on a sixth card you never look at during the talk.

words.d: you are asking me whether — a way to repeat a question before answering it
the figure, the piece of information — No tengo ese dato (I do not have that figure); los datos are the data
I am not sure — seguro agrees with the speaker: no estoy segura for a female speaker
what would happen if…? — the conditional pasaría asks about an imagined situation

look.title: Four Questions for Lucía
look.text: Classmate 1: ¿Por qué dices que las historias de tu abuela no se pueden traducir? Classmate 2: ¿Qué pasaría si tu hermano menor nunca aprendiera español? Classmate 3: ¿No crees que el inglés es más importante para conseguir trabajo? Teacher: ¿Cuántas personas hablan español en Illinois?
look.prompt: Answer each in the three-step shape. Which question should get an honest I do not have that figure, and how would you say it?

check.q: What is the first step in answering a question, according to the lesson?
check.why: Repeating the question buys time, confirms understanding, and lets the whole audience hear it.

check.q: Which is the best response to a question you cannot answer?
choices: Change the topic to your strongest reason.
Say nothing and wait for the next question.
No tengo ese dato, pero puedo buscarlo.
check.why: Admitting a gap honestly keeps the audience's trust; a guessed figure can be exposed by anyone who knows the real one.

check.q: A female speaker who is unsure should say:
choices: No estoy segura, pero creo que…
No estoy seguro, pero creo que…
No soy segura, pero creo que…
No está segura, pero creo que…
check.why: Estar is the verb for a state, the yo form is estoy, and segura agrees with a female speaker.

lessons.title: Disagreeing Politely
lessons.mainIdea: Defending a thesis means acknowledging the other view first, then holding your ground with a reason, using phrases like Entiendo su punto, pero…
reading: The classmate who asked whether English matters more was not being rude; he was doing his job. A capstone talk is *defended*, and defending means someone pushes and you do not fall over. Lucía's answer had the shape her teacher taught: "Entiendo tu punto, pero creo que las dos lenguas abren puertas diferentes." Acknowledge, then disagree, then give the reason. Skipping the first step sounds combative; skipping the third sounds stubborn.

The acknowledgment phrases are worth memorizing, and they come in two registers. To a classmate, tú: *entiendo tu punto* (I understand your point), *tienes razón en parte* (you are partly right). To a teacher or an outside judge, usted: *entiendo su punto*, *tiene razón en parte*, *respeto su opinión* (I respect your opinion). The pivot word is *pero* or, more formally, *sin embargo*. The reason follows with a connector from the last chapter or a plain porque.

Two phrases handle stronger pushback. "No estoy de acuerdo, porque…" (I do not agree, because…) is direct and fine as long as the porque comes with it. "Es cierto que…, sin embargo…" (It is true that…, however…) concedes a fact and then turns. Lucía used the second when the teacher asked whether her cousin's job was really about Spanish: "Es cierto que también tenía experiencia; sin embargo, la clínica buscaba a alguien bilingüe." (It is true that he also had experience; however, the clinic was looking for someone bilingual.) Note the personal a before alguien.

What defending is not: raising your voice, repeating the thesis louder, or agreeing with everything to make the questions stop. "Sí, tienes razón" to every challenge means you did not believe your own thesis. The audience respects a speaker who can say "tienes razón en parte" and then explain which part. Politeness and firmness are not opposites in Spanish; the phrases in this lesson hold both in one breath.

words.d: I understand your point (formal, usted) — entiendo tu punto with a classmate; the polite first step before pero
to be right — tienes razón en parte (you are partly right); Spanish has reason, it does not be right
to agree — no estoy de acuerdo (I do not agree); always add porque and a reason
it is true that — concedes a fact before a turn: Es cierto que…, sin embargo…
bilingual — the two dots on the ü mean the u is pronounced: bi-lin-güe

look.title: Three Ways to Push Back
look.text: Challenge: El español no sirve para nada en la universidad. Reply A: ¡Eso es falso! Reply B: Sí, tienes razón. Reply C: Entiendo tu punto, pero no estoy de acuerdo, porque muchas universidades de Illinois ofrecen cursos y trabajos para estudiantes bilingües. Es cierto que el inglés es necesario; sin embargo, el español es una ventaja, no un obstáculo.
look.prompt: Say what is wrong with A and with B. Then rewrite C for a teacher, changing every tú form to usted.

check.q: Which reply follows the acknowledge, disagree, reason pattern?
choices: Entiendo tu punto, pero no estoy de acuerdo, porque las dos lenguas abren puertas.
Ya lo dije en mi tesis.
check.why: The reply acknowledges, pivots with pero, and gives a reason with porque; the others attack, surrender or repeat.

check.q: How do you say "I understand your point" to a teacher, using usted?
check.why: With usted the possessive is su, not tu, and the speaker's verb stays entiendo, I understand.

check.q: What does "Es cierto que tenía experiencia; sin embargo, la clínica buscaba a alguien bilingüe" do?
choices: It agrees completely with the challenge.
It concedes a fact and then turns to hold the thesis.
check.why: Es cierto que concedes, and sin embargo turns back to the speaker's point, which is how a thesis is defended politely.

lessons.title: Reading the Rubric
lessons.mainIdea: A rubric names what the grader is listening for, so reading it before you build the talk tells you where to spend your time.
reading: Lucía's teacher handed out the *rúbrica* (rubric) the same day she assigned the talk, and the class read it before choosing topics. A rubric is a table: rows for what is being judged, columns for how well. This one has five rows, each worth four points, for twenty in all. Organization: thesis, three reasons, conclusion, transitions. Content: evidence that fits and a source for any number. Language: verb forms and agreement that are mostly right, and connectors used correctly. Delivery: notes not script, pace, eye contact. Defense: answers that acknowledge, reply and link back.

Reading the rubric tells you where the points are. Language is one row out of five; a talk with perfect grammar and no evidence scores lower than a talk with three small errors and a clear thesis. That is a relief for students who freeze over the subjunctive, and a warning for students who think fluent Spanish is enough. The rubric rewards the shape of the talk as much as the words in it.

The column descriptions matter as much as the rows. A four in Organization reads, in the teacher's Spanish, "La tesis es clara, los tres argumentos se distinguen y las transiciones guían al público" (The thesis is clear, the three reasons are distinct, and the transitions guide the audience). A two reads "Hay una tesis, pero los argumentos se mezclan" (There is a thesis, but the reasons blur together). Read your own rehearsal against those sentences and you will know your score before the teacher does.

Use the rubric while you build, not after. Lucía taped it above her desk and checked a row each night: Monday organization, Tuesday content, and so on. By Friday every row had a check mark. The rubric is not a trap set by the teacher; it is the teacher telling you, in writing, exactly how to succeed.

words.d: the rubric — the table of criteria a presentation is graded on; note the accent on the ú
the organization — thesis, three reasons, conclusion and transitions in a clear order
the content — the evidence and sources; el contenido de la presentación
the audience, the public — guiar al público (to guide the audience)
to stand apart, to be distinct — los argumentos se distinguen (the reasons are distinct from each other)

look.title: Points on the Capstone Rubric
look.cite: The example rubric described in this lesson; twenty points in all
look.prompt: A student with flawless grammar but no evidence and no transitions might score 4, 1, 4, 3, 2. What is the total, and which two rows should that student work on first?

check.q: On the example rubric, how many points is Language accuracy worth out of the total?
check.why: Each of the five rows is worth four points, so language is four out of twenty, the same weight as organization or defense.

check.q: What does "Hay una tesis, pero los argumentos se mezclan" describe?
choices: A talk with no thesis at all.
A talk with a thesis whose reasons blur together.
A talk with three clear reasons.
A talk with too many transitions.
check.why: Se mezclan means they mix or blur together, the description of a two in Organization.

check.q: Why does the lesson say to use the rubric while building the talk rather than after?
choices: Because the rubric changes after the talk.
Because the teacher collects it on Monday.
Because it tells you in advance where the points are and what to fix.
Because it is written in Spanish.
check.why: The rubric is the grader's list of what to listen for; checking each row during preparation lets you fix gaps before the talk.

lessons.title: Scoring a Classmate
lessons.mainIdea: Scoring a classmate's rehearsal against the rubric, with one comment per row in Spanish, sharpens your ear for your own talk.
reading: The week before the capstone, the class runs rehearsals in pairs. Each student scores the other on the rubric and writes one comment per row in Spanish. The comments follow the register lessons from the last unit: to a classmate, tú forms and direct suggestions. "Tu tesis es clara. Te recomiendo que hagas una pausa después de cada transición." (Your thesis is clear. I recommend that you pause after each transition.) Note hagas, the subjunctive after te recomiendo que, built from hago.

Good comments are specific and point to a fix. "Bien" (good) helps nobody. "Tu segundo argumento no tiene evidencia; añade un ejemplo o un número con fuente" (Your second reason has no evidence; add an example or a number with a source) helps immediately. The command añade is the affirmative tú form of añadir. For a suggestion softer than a command, use the subjunctive: "Sugiero que añadas un ejemplo."

Scoring someone else trains the ear. When Lucía scored Andrés, she noticed he said "en primer lugar" and then never said "en segundo lugar," so his second reason arrived unannounced. That night she checked her own cards and found the same gap. When Andrés scored Lucía, he counted seven este fillers in five minutes; she had not heard a single one. The rubric row for Delivery went from a two to a four in the next rehearsal.

The last step is to receive comments the way you want your thesis to be received: acknowledge, weigh, decide. "Entiendo tu punto sobre las pausas, y tienes razón." Some comments you will accept, some you will explain your reasons for rejecting, and both are fine. On the day of the capstone, Lucía's five cards, three reasons, one thesis and one coquí rhyme add up to a talk her grandmother, in the last row, hears every word of.

words.d: I recommend that you — a recommendation trigger; subjunctive follows: te recomiendo que hagas una pausa
to add — añade un ejemplo (add an example) is the affirmative tú command; sugiero que añadas is softer
the source — un número con fuente (a number with a source); also a fountain
the comment — un comentario por fila (one comment per row) on the rubric

look.title: Five Comments for Andrés
look.text: Organización: Tu tesis es clara, pero falta en segundo lugar antes del segundo argumento. Contenido: El tercer argumento necesita un número con fuente. Lengua: Dijiste tienen después de es importante que; debe ser tengan. Presentación: Miraste la ficha demasiado; te recomiendo que mires al público al final de cada oración. Defensa: Respondiste bien, pero no volviste a la tesis.
look.prompt: Which comment points to a grammar error, and what rule does it name? Rewrite the Presentación comment using sugiero que instead of te recomiendo que.

check.q: Te recomiendo que ___ (hacer) una pausa después de cada transición.
check.why: Te recomiendo que is a recommendation trigger with a new subject, so hacer takes the present subjunctive hagas, from hago.

check.q: Which comment is most useful to a classmate?
choices: Tu segundo argumento no tiene evidencia; añade un número con fuente.
check.why: A useful comment names the problem and points to a specific fix; the others are vague praise or vague orders.

check.q: What does "Miraste la ficha demasiado" mean?
choices: You looked at the card too much.
You wrote too much on the card.
check.why: Miraste is the tú preterite of mirar, to look at, and demasiado means too much.

review.q: Which sentence is a thesis, not a fact?
choices: Mi abuela es de Puerto Rico.
Sostengo que las escuelas de Illinois deben ofrecer más cursos de español.
review.why: A thesis takes a position that could be argued; the other three are plain facts.

review.q: Creo que el español ___ (ser) una ventaja en mi barrio.
review.why: Creo que states a belief the speaker stands behind and keeps the indicative es; only no creo que would take sea.

review.q: Which phrase opens the first supporting reason?
review.why: En primer lugar means in the first place and announces the first reason.

review.q: What is the best way to handle a question whose answer you do not know?
choices: Say honestly that you do not have that figure and can look it up.
review.why: An honest gap keeps trust; a guessed figure can be wrong and exposed.

review.q: Which reply defends a thesis politely?
choices: Sí, tienes razón, olvida mi tesis.
Entiendo tu punto, pero no estoy de acuerdo, porque…
review.why: Acknowledge, disagree, give a reason: that is the polite and firm pattern for defending a point.

review.q: What does "Pasemos ahora a la conclusión" mean?
choices: Let us move now to the conclusion.
review.why: Pasemos is the nosotros command of pasar, let us move, used as a transition that includes the audience.

review.q: Why should a speaker use index cards instead of a full script?
choices: Cards let you look at the audience and speak instead of read.
Scripts are not allowed in Spanish.
Scripts must be written in English.
review.why: Notes keep the eyes up and the voice alive; the teacher's note was No lo leas. Habla.

review.q: On a five-row rubric with four points per row, a score of 4, 3, 2, 4, 3 totals how many out of twenty?
review.why: 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 4 plus 3 equals 16 out of 20.
